splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Sixth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running during the period of absconding.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory basis for the fugitive tolling doctrine in this context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) from raising any claim they previously presented in a successive § 2255 motion, or whether they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law. The outcome determines how strict the gatekeeping requirements are for federal prisoners seeking successive collateral attacks on their convictions.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy the requirements in § 2255(h) itself.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether and when candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split affects how courts evaluate standing for candidates challenging election rules before an election takes place, with implications for challenges to mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge state election laws that allegedly dilute the value of lawfully cast votes, including laws permitting late-arriving ballots.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized interest in fair elections is insufficient to establish the concrete, particularized injury required by Article III for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal sentencing consequences.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether courts should apply the rule of lenity or defer to an agency's (or the Sentencing Commission's) interpretation when a criminal sentencing provision is ambiguous. At least three circuits hold that lenity prevails over deference, while the Third Circuit held that agency deference trumps lenity. This split affects how sentencing enhancements are interpreted and has deepened following Loper Bright's overruling of Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over Auer/Kisor deference or Chevron deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference prevails over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines enhancements with criminal sentencing consequences.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether any single criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to vastly different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on which circuit they are in.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' conjunctively.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and other inchoate offenses, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary in Application Note 1—which adds inchoate offenses like conspiracy to the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes—is a valid, authoritative interpretation deserving deference, or impermissibly expands the text of § 4B1.2(b). This split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify as career offenders.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is the Sentencing Commission's authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) and properly includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy within the definition of 'controlled substance offense.'

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text and is not entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline's scope beyond its plain text, so it does not deserve Kisor deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule of controlled substances is broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance underlying the state conviction to also be controlled under federal law. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require a match to the federal schedule. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the particular substance is controlled under federal law.

positions.label: Federal-law limitation applies — substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law—alone or in combination with other factors—as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Eighth Circuit categorically prohibits this, while other circuits and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) permit it. This affects prisoners serving lengthy sentences under laws Congress has since reformed.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot contribute to extraordinary and compelling reasons
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons warranting a sentence reduction, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions regarding conditions or execution of a sentence (such as transfer to prerelease custody under the First Step Act) must be brought as a habeas corpus petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or may also be brought as a civil rights action.
splits.description: Circuits have long been divided on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy for prisoner challenges that do not directly contest the fact or duration of confinement but rather the conditions or execution of a sentence. This split affects whether prisoners challenging BOP decisions on earned time credits, halfway house placement, and other First Step Act benefits can proceed via habeas or must use civil rights statutes.

positions.label: Habeas is the proper vehicle for challenges to execution of sentence
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions regarding the execution of a sentence, including First Step Act time credit applications and transfer to prerelease custody, are properly brought as habeas corpus petitions under § 2241.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Woodall v. Federal Bureau of Prisons

positions.label: Conditions-of-confinement claims may proceed outside habeas
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement or certain aspects of sentence execution that do not challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may be brought outside habeas, including via Bivens or the APA.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an appeal from the denial of a motion for attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter (subject to a 30-day appeal deadline) or a criminal matter (subject to a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, but acknowledged the split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to explicitly punish defendants for the conduct underlying supervised release violations, placing it at odds with other circuits that hold revocation sentences should be based on the breach of the court's trust rather than as punishment for new criminal conduct. Dissenting judges in the Sixth Circuit noted this places the circuit at the extreme of a split.

positions.label: Courts may punish for the underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences as punishment for the defendant's violation of supervised release conditions, including the underlying criminal conduct.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must focus on breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sanctions should be calibrated to the seriousness of the breach of the court's trust, not as additional punishment for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value between the original Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtors. The Ninth Circuit held such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with other circuits that hold the appreciation belongs to the converting debtors. This affects debtors' incentives to convert cases and the distribution of assets to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and § 541(a) means that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtors, consistent with the statute's purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as a decision 'effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.'
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order,' while other circuits have been more restrictive about when sealed-record denials qualify for interlocutory appeal. This affects litigants' ability to protect sensitive health information during ongoing litigation.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because they can be adequately remedied on appeal from final judgment or through other mechanisms.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: In re City of New York

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied differing standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, leading to inconsistent results regarding liability and available remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, which impacts hospitality, retail, and other service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for discrimination claims against business operators, allowing broader theories of liability and remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard that limits the scope of actionable discrimination claims and available remedies against business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
